value.overview: The Golden-browed Chlorophonia (Chlorophonia callophrys) is a small, colorful finch of the humid mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is especially associated with mossy cloud forests, where it searches the canopy and forest edges for berries. Males have vivid green and yellow plumage with a dark, blue-violet crown and a golden eyebrow. Females are generally duller and less strongly marked. In Costa Rica, it is a familiar resident of montane forests.
value.classification: The Golden-browed Chlorophonia belongs to the order Passeriformes and the finch family Fringillidae. Its scientific name is Chlorophonia callophrys.
value.identification: This small, compact bird has a short, thick bill and bright green upperparts. The male has a blue-violet crown, a broad golden-yellow eyebrow, dark facial markings, yellow underparts, and green flanks. The female is less vivid, with a greener and more subdued head pattern. Both sexes have dark wings edged in green and a rounded appearance. It is often detected in the canopy by its soft, clear whistles and short, nasal contact notes.
value.rangeHabitat: The Golden-browed Chlorophonia occurs along the mountain ranges of Costa Rica and extends into western Panama, particularly Chiriquí and nearby areas. In Costa Rica it is distributed widely through the montane ranges, including humid highland forests on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes. It favors evergreen cloud forest, forest interior, edges, and partially open areas with mature trees, moss, bromeliads, and other epiphytes. It generally occurs from roughly 900 or 1,000 meters to the upper tree line, with local seasonal movements to lower elevations.
value.migrationStatus: It is primarily a resident species in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local or elevational movements, especially after breeding or when fruit is scarce at higher elevations. On the Caribbean slope of Costa Rica, birds may descend noticeably during some seasons.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding generally occurs from February through June, and two broods may sometimes be attempted. Both adults help construct a roughly spherical nest with a side entrance, usually using moss and placing it among bromeliads or other epiphytes on a tree trunk or branch. The clutch contains at least three pale eggs marked with reddish-brown blotches. The female incubates, while both parents feed the nestlings, mainly by regurgitating food.
value.dietFeeding: The Golden-browed Chlorophonia feeds mainly on small fruits and berries, including mistletoe fruits and figs, with insects making up only a minor part of the diet. It usually forages high in the forest canopy and may visit fruiting trees along forest edges. During the breeding season it is commonly seen in pairs. At other times, several birds may gather in small groups of up to about a dozen individuals.
value.behavior: This active chlorophonia moves quietly through leafy branches while searching for fruit. It sometimes associates with other birds at fruiting trees but only occasionally joins mixed-species feeding flocks. Outside the breeding period, small groups may form and later separate into pairs. Its vocalizations include a distinctive, soft whistle and short contact calls. Because it often remains in the canopy and blends with mossy vegetation, it may be easier to hear than to see.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, although the species remains common in Costa Rica and is less common in its smaller Panamanian range.
